texts.preamble: M/S. Parekh Foods Ltd., New Delhi Ano vs Food Inspector, Jagityal Municipality on 23 February, 2022 Author: Chillakur Sumalatha Bench: Chillakur Sumalatha Honourable Dr. Justice Chillakur Sumalatha Criminal Petition No.10163 of 2014 Order:
texts.facts: 3. The Food Inspector, Jagtial Municipality, presented a complaint before the Court of Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Jagtial, contending that the accused committed the offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, which would hereinafter be referred as 'PFA Act, 1954' for brevity. Cognizance was taken for the said Dr.CSL , J offence and thereby, the criminal proceedings commenced against the accused including the petitioners herein. The proceedings initiated are challenged on the ground that no case is made out against them by the respondent. They seek to quash the proceedings. 5. The version of the complainant, as could be perceived through the contents of the complaint, is that on 01.03.2004, the Food Inspector, Jagtial Municipality, inspected M/s. Chitumalla Laxminarayana Kiran & General Store, Jagtial, and found Samrat groundnut oil packets one litre each, 20 in number, kept for sale. Disclosing his name and address particulars and in the presence of witness, the Food Inspector purchased three sealed packets of the said groundnut oil by paying Dr.CSL , J price. The said groundnut oil was divided into parts, sealed and labelled as provided under law. One part of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis. On analysis, the Public Analyst submitted his report duly mentioning that the declaration "Representative sample tested in M/S. Parekh Foods Ltd., New Delhi Ano vs Food Inspector, Jagityal Municipality on 23 February, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/70884880/ 1 competent laboratory and certified unadulterated" is misbranded. Thus, the accused, who are responsible for the said misbranding, are liable for punishment. 6. Making a submission that the narration over the sample that the 'representative sample tested in competent laboratory and certified unadulterated', is not misbranded, learned counsel for the petitioners/ accused Nos.3 and 4 contended that there is no averment in the analyst report showing the basis on which the said observation is made by the Public Analyst and the said fact itself vitiates the proceedings.
texts.arguments: Heard the submission of Sri Rajesh Batra, who has submitted his contentions on behalf of Sri S. Niranjan Reddy, learned counsel appearing for the petitioners, as well as learned Assistant Public Prosecutor representing the respondent. 2. Seeking to quash the proceedings that are pending against the petitioners in C.C.No.1125 of 2008 on the file of the Court of Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Jagtial, the petitioners, who are arrayed as accused Nos.3 and 4 in the said Calender Case, are before this Court. Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 is an Dr.CSL , J enactment which is legislated to prohibit manufacture, storing, sale or distribution of any adulterated and misbranded food. Section 2 (ix) narrates the circumstances where an article of food shall be deemed to be misbranded. As per Section 2 (ix) (e), an article of food shall be deemed to be misbranded if false claims are made upon the label or otherwise. 8. In the case on hand, the version of the complainant is that the declaration that the 'representative sample is tested in competent laboratory and was certified to be unadulterated' is misbrand. Learned counsel for the petitioner in this regard submitted that there was no requirement for testing the groundnut oil in the competent laboratory for sale in the erstwhile State of Andhra Pradesh, but such a requirement was there at Union Territory Delhi during that time i.e., in the year 2004 and as the product was being sold in the entire country, the representative sample of the product was got tested in the competent Dr.CSL , J laboratory and was put for sale in the entire country and therefore, the product that was sold in the erstwhile State of Andhra Pradesh also contained the said endorsement that the 'representative sample was tested in competent laboratory and certified unadulterated'. Learned counsel for the petitioners has further drawn the attention of this Court to the contents of Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, more particularly Rule 7. 9. Rule 7 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules 1955, which would hereinafter be referred as 'PFA Rules, 1955', for brevity, envisages the duties of Public Analyst. Discussing all these aspects and also the powers of the Court to quash the proceedings, the Honourable Apex Court in the case between STATE OF HARYANA vs. BHAJAN LAL1, at para 102, held as follows: "In the backdrop of the interpretation of the various relevant provisions of the Code under Chapter XIV and of the principles of law enunciated by this Court in a series of decisions relating to the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code which which we have extracted and reproduced above, we give the following categories of cases by way of illustration wherein such power could be exercised either (1992) Supp. (1) SCC 335 Dr.CSL , J to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, though it may not be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and sufficiently channelized and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases wherein such power should be exercised. (1) Where the allegations made in the first information report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused. (2) Where the allegations in the first information report and other materials, if any, accompanying the FIR do not disclose a cognizable offence, justifying an investigation by police officers under Section 156(1) of the Code except under an order of a Magistrate within the purview of Section 155(2) of the Code. (3) Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused. (4) Where, the allegations in the M/S. Parekh Foods Ltd., New Delhi Ano vs Food Inspector, Jagityal Municipality on 23 February, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/70884880/ 3 FIR do not constitute a cognizable offence but constitute only a non-cognizable offence, no investigation is permitted by a police office without an order of a Magistrate as contemplated under Section 155(2) of the Code. (5) Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused. Dr.CSL , J (6) Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act (under which a criminal proceeding is instituted) to the institution and continuance of the proceedings and/or where there is a specific provision in the Code or the concerned Act, providing efficacious redress for the grievance of the aggrieved party. (7) Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge."
